title: Home or office? The impact of home and office attributes on workplace decisions in hybrid working
research_question: This study investigated the impact of seven office and six home workplace attributes on choice behaviour.

participants.description: Employees from three Dutch municipalities in The Netherlands (Almere, Amsterdam, Eindhoven). 57.7% Female, 40.5% Male. Age distribution: 18-35 (20.5%), 36-45 (21.6%), 46-55 (28.0%), 55+ (30.0%).
participants.recruitment: Employees were invited via a link to an online survey provided by their respective employers. Participation was voluntary.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two rendered images showcasing the kitchenette and workspace, with aesthetic elements embedded. Other attributes were described in text. Participants were presented with six choice combinations (choice sets) in a hybrid workday scenario.

measures.construct: Workplace choice behavior (preference for office, home, or no preference)
measures.instrument: Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) analyzed with Multinomial Logit (MNL) and Random Parameter Mixed Logit (RPML) models

findings.antecedent: Choosing 'no preference' option
findings.mechanism: experimental setup effectively encouraged participants to make specific choices rather than opting out.
findings.quote: The utility of choosing 'no preference' was negative (βn=-6.168), suggesting that the workplace options were clearly defined

findings.antecedent: Office shared with direct colleagues
findings.mechanism: fosters interaction and collaboration
findings.quote: Direct colleagues in the office environment had a significant positive mean part-worth utility value (βdirect-colleagues=+0.697)

findings.antecedent: Office shared with others (non-direct colleagues)
findings.quote: (implied from direct colleagues finding due to effect coding)

findings.antecedent: Commuting time between office and home within 15 min
findings.mechanism: most strongly reduced the attractiveness of the home alternative
findings.quote: A commuting time of less than 15 min (β<15min = -0.735) most strongly reduced the attractiveness of the home alternative

findings.antecedent: Commuting time between office and home between 15-30 min
findings.mechanism: also reduced the appeal of the home alternative
findings.quote: followed by a commute time of between 15 and 30 min (β15-30 min = -0.395), which also reduced the appeal of the home alternative.

findings.antecedent: Commuting time between office and home between 30-45 min
findings.mechanism: generally increased the appeal of the home-workplace
findings.quote: a commuting time of between 30 and 45 min (β30-45 min = + 0.274; σ30-45 = 0.747) generally increased the appeal of the home-workplace

findings.antecedent: Commuting time between office and home more than 45 min
findings.mechanism: had an even greater influence on encouraging participants to choose the home-workplace
findings.quote: A commuting time of more than 45 min (β>45 min = + 0.856) had an even greater influence on encouraging participants to choose the home-workplace

findings.antecedent: Having an ergonomic workstation at home
findings.mechanism: made participants more likely to choose the home-workplace
findings.quote: An ergonomic workstation at home (βergonomic = + 0.414) made participants more likely to choose the home-workplace

findings.antecedent: Not having an ergonomic workstation at home
findings.quote: (implied from ergonomic workstation finding due to effect coding)

findings.antecedent: Having a dedicated workroom (separate room) at home
findings.mechanism: made participants more likely to choose the home-workplace
findings.quote: Participants were more likely to choose the home-workplace when they had a dedicated workroom (βa workroom = + 0.334) at home.

findings.antecedent: Having a dedicated work area (but not a separate room) at home
findings.mechanism: for half of the participants, a dedicated work area made the home alternative more appealing, while for the other half, it did not.
findings.quote: The mean value of a dedicated work area (but not a separate room) was around zero with a significant standard deviation of 1.298.

findings.antecedent: Having a non-specific home location (e.g., dining table) for work
findings.mechanism: Participants were less likely to choose the home-workplace
findings.quote: Participants were less likely to choose the home-workplace when they had a non-specific home location (βnon-specific = -0.323), such as a dining table.

findings.antecedent: Others (family members/housemates) present at home during workday
findings.mechanism: most participants were less likely to choose the home-workplace
findings.quote: most participants were less likely to choose the home-workplace when others (βothers present = -0.301) were present at home.

findings.antecedent: Others (family members/housemates) not present at home during workday
findings.quote: (implied from others present finding due to effect coding)

findings.antecedent: Living in an apartment
findings.mechanism: Approximately half of the participants showed a negative preference for the apartment
findings.quote: Approximately half of the participants showed a negative preference for the apartment, semi-detached, or row-houses

findings.antecedent: Living in a semi-detached or row house
findings.mechanism: Approximately half of the participants showed a negative preference for the apartment, semi-detached, or row-houses
findings.quote: Approximately half of the participants showed a negative preference for the apartment, semi-detached, or row-houses

findings.antecedent: Living in a detached house
findings.mechanism: participants were more likely to work at home when they had their home-workplace in a detached house.
findings.quote: The part worth utility for a detached house was 0.175 (βdetached house), suggesting that participants were more likely to work at home when they had their home-workplace in a detached house.

findings.antecedent: Employer-supplied smart technology at home (digital tools, meeting equipment, fast internet)
findings.mechanism: made the home-workplace more appealing for all participants.
findings.quote: smart technology showing a significant positive utility value (βsmart tech. = + 0.131) and no significant variations among participants, meaning that smart technology made the home-workplace more appealing for all participants.

findings.antecedent: Basic/regular technology at home
findings.quote: (implied from smart technology finding due to effect coding)

findings.antecedent: No events held at the office
findings.mechanism: Participants were less likely to prefer the office-workplace when no-events were held
findings.quote: Participants were less likely to prefer the office-workplace when no-events (βno-events = -0.458) were held at the office.

findings.antecedent: Social events (networking, team drinks) held at the office
findings.mechanism: increased the office appeal for all participants.
findings.quote: Participants preferred the office-workplace more when social events (βsocial = + 0.247) or wellness events (βwellness = + 0.211) were presented in the office alternative.

findings.antecedent: Wellness events (mindfulness, fitness, talks) held at the office
findings.mechanism: increased the office appeal for all participants.
findings.quote: Participants preferred the office-workplace more when social events (βsocial = + 0.247) or wellness events (βwellness = + 0.211) were presented in the office alternative.

findings.antecedent: Kitchenette-only option at the office
findings.mechanism: discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.
findings.quote: An office with a kitchenette-only option (βonly-kitch. = -0.340) discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: Kitchenette with standing tables at the office
findings.mechanism: did not have any influence on choice decisions.
findings.quote: a kitchenette with standing tables (βstanding tables = +0.000) did not have any influence on choice decisions.

findings.antecedent: Kitchenette with sitting area at the office
findings.mechanism: encouraged participants to choose the office-workplace.
findings.quote: a kitchenette with a sitting area (βsitting = + 0.168) and with a sitting & gaming area (βsitting&gaming = + 0.172) encouraged participants to choose the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: Kitchenette with sitting and gaming area at the office
findings.mechanism: encouraged participants to choose the office-workplace.
findings.quote: a kitchenette with a sitting area (βsitting = + 0.168) and with a sitting & gaming area (βsitting&gaming = + 0.172) encouraged participants to choose the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: Smart technology at the office (interactive screens, smart workstation, meeting table with touchscreen)
findings.mechanism: enhanced the appeal of the office-workplace
findings.quote: Smart technology (βsmart tech. = +0.163) enhanced the appeal of the office-workplace over the home-workplace for all participants

findings.antecedent: Basic/regular technology at the office
findings.mechanism: discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.
findings.quote: basic technology (βbasic tech. = -0.163) discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: Single-office with non-transparent walls
findings.mechanism: roughly half of the participants preferred this type of office, while the other half did not.
findings.quote: For single offices with solid-walls, the mean utility was around zero (βsingle-solid walls = + 0.004), suggesting no impact on choice decisions, but the significant standard deviation (σsingle-solid walls=1.024) indicates that roughly half of the participants preferred this type of office, while the other half did not.

findings.antecedent: Single-office with one glass wall
findings.mechanism: encouraged the majority of participants to prefer the office-workplace
findings.quote: single offices with a glass-wall (βsingle-glass-wall = + 0.169) encouraged the majority of participants to prefer the office-workplace

findings.antecedent: Open-office with half-wall separation
findings.mechanism: somewhat discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.
findings.quote: Both kinds of open-offices, with half-walls (βopen-half-walls = -0.088) and with no-separation (βopen-no sepr = -0.085), somewhat discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: Open-office with no separation
findings.mechanism: somewhat discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.
findings.quote: Both kinds of open-offices, with half-walls (βopen-half-walls = -0.088) and with no-separation (βopen-no sepr = -0.085), somewhat discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: Reservation is required for a workseat at the office
findings.mechanism: discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace
findings.quote: If a reservation is required for a workseat (βrequired = -0.068), it discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace

findings.antecedent: Reservation is not possible for a workseat at the office
findings.quote: (implied from reservation required finding due to effect coding)

findings.antecedent: Office aesthetics with warm colours, plants, art objects
findings.mechanism: all participants had a neutral preference for office aesthetics
findings.quote: aesthetics at the office-workplace showed no significant impact on choice behaviour with both levels

findings.antecedent: Office aesthetics with cool colours, no plants, no art objects
findings.mechanism: all participants had a neutral preference for office aesthetics
findings.quote: aesthetics at the office-workplace showed no significant impact on choice behaviour with both levels

mechanisms: Reduced stress and physical discomfort (e.g., ergonomic workstation, shorter commute)
Increased social interaction and bonding (e.g., direct colleagues, social events, sitting/gaming areas in kitchenette)
Improved task performance and reduced cognitive load (e.g., smart technology, no reservation required)
Privacy regulation (e.g., dedicated workroom, absence of others at home, single offices vs. open plan)
Restoration and well-being (e.g., wellness events, sitting/gaming areas in kitchenette)
Autonomy in workplace choice (general benefit of hybrid working)
moderators: Unobserved heterogeneity in preferences (indicated by significant standard deviations in RPML for many attributes)
Commuting time (differential impact on home preference)
Office occupant type (direct vs. non-direct colleagues)
Workspace type (single office vs. open plan, dedicated workroom vs. non-specific home location)
Type of dwelling (apartment vs. detached house)
implementation_implications: Organisations should invest in well-designed shared secondary office spaces rather than focusing solely on individual workstations.
Provide office-workplaces with organised social or wellness events, functional secondary space designs, smart technology, and shorter commutes.
Support employees with ergonomic workstations and smart technology in their home workplaces.
Foster an environment where employees can work alongside their direct colleagues to enhance workplace appeal and encourage office attendance.
Consider multi-functional spaces that can accommodate office events and activities beyond standard desk-based work.
Facility managers should consider smart technology features when designing and presenting office workplaces.
Future housing design should align with individuals' needs, considering hybrid work contexts.
Workplace policies and office layouts should be designed to support team co-location.
Autonomy in workplace choice within hybrid work arrangements can enhance productivity and satisfaction.

tables.description: Extending Hall's proximity concept to hybrid workplace environments at the office and home.
Systematically varied workplace attributes and their relevant levels used in the DCE design.
Workplace attributes and their levels included in the additional survey questions regarding participants' own existing home workplace setup (home situation individual-based).
Overview of the sample and individual-based home situation data collected.
Spearman's rank correlation coefficients among home-situation attributes.
Participants' current type of work requirement.
Multinomial logit model and Random parameter mixed logit model results for workplace choice.

limitations: Sample limited to civil servants from three Dutch municipalities, restricting generalizability to other types of office workers or organizational cultures.
Findings based on hypothetical DCE scenarios, which may not fully capture real-world office environment complexities.
Participants may have evaluated familiar office attributes more reliably than unfamiliar ones.
Explicitly asked participants to assume no home obligations, but such responsibilities may nonetheless influence real-world workplace choices.
Did not examine personal characteristics (e.g., gender, age, education level) as moderators for heterogeneity in workplace preferences.
Examined only eleven home and office attributes; future studies should explore additional attributes.
Public space (E3) zone included only commuting time; future research should incorporate additional attributes related to public space (e.g., neighborhood characteristics, nearby shops, green spaces).
Aesthetics assessed by combining three elements (colour, presence of art and greenery); future studies should investigate them separately.
